description:
We are a multidisciplinary team of students and educators from Cochabamba, a valley in the Bolivian Andes where farmers grow potatoes, maize, fava beans, wheat and alfalfa while facing frost, drought and increasingly late rains.

Our goal is to turn NASA data (NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, SMAP, MODIS NDVI) and local information from the Municipal Government of Cochabamba into a simple, Spanish-first web tool that ranks crop rotations by soil health, climate risk and each farmer’s priorities.
summary: Yatiri X is a web platform, in Spanish and Quechua, that helps small farmers in the valleys and peri-urban areas of Cochabamba, Bolivia, decide what to sow, when, and with how much water. A farmer marks the plot on a map and says what was sown; Yatiri X combines 45 years of NASA POWER climate data, NASA SRTM elevation, SMAP, GPM IMERG and MODIS layers, the municipality's official zoning layers and a 31-scenario probabilistic forecast. It recommends a three-year crop rotation, the best sowing week, the irrigation needed (FAO-56), and shows frost, drought, waterlogging and erosion risks, pests and care for 147 crops. Tiri, an AI assistant, answers questions using only the plot's data. It matters because irregular rains, frost and repeated crops make families lose harvests, water and soil; Yatiri X turns open NASA data into clear, local advice that anyone can read, at three levels of detail.
details:
WHAT IT DOES. Yatiri X ("We know your land, we grow a better future") is decision support for small farmers in Cochabamba, Bolivia. The farmer marks a plot (GPS, one tap, corner by corner or traced with a finger), says what was sown (several crops, or "Other", which AI analyses) and what water is available. Yatiri X then shows: the best three-year crop rotation with an explained score (climate 45, rotation 30, soil 10, priorities 15); the best sowing week for each of 147 crops; crop water needs and irrigation (FAO-56 Penman-Monteith and crop coefficients); a probabilistic forecast for days, weeks and months ("6 in 10 scenarios bring frost tonight"); frost, drought, waterlogging and erosion risks with what to do and not do; 64 pests and diseases, 16 invasive species and 12 home remedies with real photos; 3D terrain; comparison between several plots; a PDF report; and Tiri, an AI assistant.

HOW IT WORKS. NASA POWER daily data 1981-2025 is adjusted to each plot's altitude from NASA SRTM. A deterministic engine evaluates every crop and every sowing week over 45 years, then scores thousands of rotations. Forecast probabilities come from the NOAA GFS 31-member ensemble compared with the NASA climatology. The municipality's official layers (peri-urban zones, drainage, districts) are read for each plot.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT. Less irrigation water (for example about 2,900 m3 per hectare in three years in District 9), fewer frost losses, healthier soil by rotating with legumes, and early warnings. Built for the municipality and for people who prefer Quechua.

CREATIVITY. Three reading levels (simple words, medium, advanced with numbers); the whole site in Quechua; crop names translated (maize = sara); "Other" crops estimated by AI; automatic daily bulletins with n8n; a living, animated interface.

TOOLS. HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no build step), Leaflet, three.js, Node.js, Netlify (site, functions and scheduled jobs), Supabase (optional accounts), n8n (automations), Gemini API, NASA GIBS.

FACTORS CONSIDERED. Weak mobile signal (light pages), low literacy (simple view, icons, Quechua), honesty (when data is missing the app says so), privacy (plots stay on the device unless the user creates an account), and validation (crop values marked for review with INIAF and SENASAG).
